Hegseth vows to keep fighting from Pentagon, defends Iran war

Democrats, who won control of US Congress in the midterm elections, have promised to investigate US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon.

WASHINGTON: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday (Nov 5) vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as “courageous and historic” after voters punished Republicans over it in this week’s midterm elections . Hegseth's remarks, posted on social media, came as taunts from his foes in Congress intensified and President Donald Trump swatted away questions about whether he might fire Hegseth . Trump has commended his Pentagon chief. The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, asked in a post: "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?" Hegseth, a former Fox News host, has been a polarising figure who has made enemies even within his own Republican Party. Critics in Congress are targeting his conduct of the Iran war, which Vice President JD Vance has said cost Republicans control of Congress, his firing of top military officers and strained relations with lawmakers as the administration seeks a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package. Democrats, who won control of Congress in Tuesday's elections, have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and congressional aides say that would include the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, among other issues. Republican Representative Thomas Massie promised to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth next week, warning that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for him once Republicans cede control of Congress next year to Democrats. "They’ll have hearings & trials," Massie wrote on X. Hegseth defended his stewardship of the Pentagon in a more than four-minute video that boasted about firing senior Pentagon leaders, ending diversity initiatives and banning transgender individuals from the military. "You see, they attack me - they attack us - because we are effective. It's not going to work. We will not back down," Hegseth said to the camera. Calling the impeachment effort a "sham," Hegseth said that Trump himself was impeached twice. "It's all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that," he said. Trump on Thursday praised Hegseth when asked whether he expected any staffing changes, saying his defence secretary had "done a fantastic job" and suggesting that the opposition to him was tied to his firing of generals. "We had so many generals. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it. And many of those people were woke. I don't like a woke general. And so, he probably has opposition," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. Trump also praised Hegseth's role in US military operations in Venezuela and Iran. "Venezuela has been unbelievable ... and in Iran, we are there for seven months and we control everything that we've wanted to control," he said.

Related:

Republicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing

Trump says Hegseth doing 'a very good job' as questions swirl about his future

CHOPPING BLOCK Sources have said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their election losses. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress, in extraordinary remarks that raised questions about whether Trump might still go ahead with a threatened resumption of major combat operations against Iran. One Trump adviser said Hegseth "could be on the chopping block" because of the Iran war. The Defense Department has said Hegseth is "100 per cent committed" to leading the Pentagon until the end of Trump's term. Hegseth appealed to "patriotic" lawmakers to pass a funding request that aims to help the Pentagon pay for the Iran war and other spending priorities. "Regardless of how people feel about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets nuclear weapons, we need to continue, as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military," Hegseth said. Republican US Senator Thom Tillis told CBS on Tuesday night that Hegseth has "a reckoning" coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package in Congress. Hegseth could also face scrutiny from Democrats over his Ukraine policy and US military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes. Representative Adam Smith, the Democrat who is expected to lead the House Armed Services Committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything from the Iran war to what he called the erosion of the "apolitical foundation of the armed forces".

Source: Reuters/nh

WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday (Nov 5) dismissed reports that he was planning to leave the Trump administration as he weighs his next moves after Republicans' losses in midterm elections, according to The New York Times. It has "always been my plan" to work for President Donald Trump until the end of his term, Rubio told The Times in an interview. Rubio, who also serves as Trump's national security adviser, is widely considered a potential successor to Trump in the 2028 presidential race. Just days before Tuesday's midterm elections, he made an unusual appearance alongside the US leader on the campaign trail, briefly stepping up on the podium to address a cheering crowd at a rally.

Rubio declined to answer questions about his political future on Thursday, however, saying: "I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore." On reports that he was considering an exit from the Trump administration, he told The New York Times: "I don't know where these things come from, to be honest with you." Earlier Thursday, Bloomberg News reported that Rubio was weighing whether to leave the administration. The report added that Rubio spoke to White House officials about stepping down, and was asked to stay. But the State Department has hit back sharply against reports that Rubio might leave. Dylan Johnson, Assistant Secretary of State for global public affairs, called the Bloomberg article "totally made up". He also called a report by news outlet The Independent, which said Rubio was planning to launch a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, "completely baseless fake news". Rubio has previously said that he would support Vice President JD Vance if he ran for president. Vance is also widely considered a possible 2028 candidate.

LONDON: Ukraine's renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries add to Moscow's difficulty in addressing domestic fuel shortages while it ships diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump. The Ryazan oil refinery , one of R us sia's largest, appeared to have come under attack as part of a large drone strike overnight on ind us trial sites in the city, southeast of Moscow, according to a Reuters video analysis. If confirmed, it would be the second refinery to be hit this week following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant, northeast of Moscow, overnight on Monday (Nov 2), marking the breakdown of a pa us e in strikes. Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries this year forced large amounts of processing capacity in western R us sia offline, ca us ing fuel shortages that meant Moscow had to enforce fuel export bans from April onwards.

A ban on diesel exports has been lifted in part and the US struck the deal in October with the Kremlin to resume diesel exports to international markets when Trump was seeking to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on Nov 3, which Trump's Republican Party lost . The city of Ryazan had restored power supply earlier on Thursday as fires at the unnamed ind us trial sites were either contained or put out, the local governor said on social media.

US -R US SIA DIESEL CARGOES ARE IN FOC US At least six Russian diesel cargoes have broadcast that they plan transatlantic voyages, shipping data from Kpler and LSEG show, while two cargoes appeared to have changed course after being previo us ly bound for the US Atlantic coast. No Russian diesel cargo has arrived in the US since the deal , the data show. The first observed US -bound Russian shipment is expected to arrive in New York this weekend, but regulatory, legislative and sanctions concerns mean that its discharge is not guaranteed, Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. "These are commercial loadings, so naturally the details cannot be made public. All the diesel will find its buyers," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call. Tankers often broadcast messages known as signals, such as "Atlantic coast for orders", indicating they are heading for the US Atlantic coast but have no confirmed discharge port, so the crew is awaiting instructions. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russian diesel cargoes destined for the US are continuing on course, in a post on X. There is no connection between diesel tankers changing course and the result of the US midterm elections, Peskov added.

New wave of bomb hoaxes hits at least 27 passenger flights across Europe

While no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks".

PARIS: Hoax bomb threat s disrupted at least 27 passenger flights across Europe on Thursday (Nov 5), forcing unplanned landings by some planes and prompting fighter jets to escort or intercept others, in the second such wave this week. No country has attributed blame for the threat s, which come as many European officials are accusing Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks" , often cheap, easily deniable and not expected to trigger an armed response. At least seven flights and a cruise ship also received hoax threat s on Tuesday. Denmark, Poland and Romania, all affected by Thursday's disruptions, have previously accused Moscow directly of being behind hybrid attacks, while Germany blamed Russia for an August attack on Leipzig airport. Britain , which has in the past blamed Russia, linked Iran to a suspected plot against a US air base. Both Russia and Iran deny any involvement. Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, said most of the countries affected supported Ukraine in its war against Russia's invasion. While analysts at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said a link to Russia's hybrid campaign in Europe was a "realistic probability", they also cautioned that other explanations, including individuals acting on personal grievances and copycat incidents, were also possible. An airport source in Italy told Reuters that an email with the subject line " Threat report" had been sent to several addresses for airlines, airport operators and airport service providers at Rome's Fiumicino and Milan's Malpensa airports. The email, which claimed it was from "fighters of the Male State", said devices had been placed on inbound flights from Helsinki and Dublin and they would explode in 60 minutes. Reuters could not independently confirm who had sent the email and there was no immediate indication of who was behind the other threat s across Europe.

FROM MILAN TO PRAGUE AND BEYOND Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome landed safely at Evreux airport, 100km west of Paris, after being diverted as a security precaution, the Irish airline said in a statement. Quoting the office of French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, Reuters reported that the Airbus A320 plane was diverted to France's Evreux airbase. The situation is being monitored by the Prime Minister's office, it added. According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, an Aer Lingus aircraft turned near Paris and was circling over the Evreux area after declaring an in-flight emergency. France's air force said it had dispatched planes "as soon as the threat was reported", AFP reported.  "The aircraft has been diverted and is being escorted to the Evreux airfield" west of Paris, it added.

An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat, France on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Gonzalo Fuentes)

A Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by charter airline Jettime, on Thursday landed as normal in Vienna after receiving a bomb threat , a spokesperson for the Finnish carrier said. Finnair earlier said that another Finnair flight to Rome had landed after receiving a bomb threat, Reuters reported. According to AFP, t he Helsinki-Rome flight was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts. Reuters, citing a source, reported that a flight operated by Polish airline LOT flying from Warsaw landed safely at Brussels Airport following a suspicious report. A spokesperson for the airport told Belgian media that no additional security measures were necessary. The airport did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

A view of Fiumicino Airport, after a Finnair plane from Helsinki was safely escorted to its scheduled landing in Rome by Italian air force jets following bomb threats that forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe, in Fiumicino, near Rome, Italy on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Remo Casilli)

Bulgarian officials meanwhile reported three aircraft making emergency landings in the Balkan country because of bomb threats. Airplanes flying from Copenhagen and Madrid landed safely in Sofia, the interior minister said, according to broadcaster bTV. A third aircraft, from London, was diverted and landed in Plovdiv, Bulgaria's second-largest city, local media said. The government did not respond to requests for comment. Spanish authorities said that three flights were affected by hoax bomb threats at Madrid's airport on Thursday morning, though they stressed that security forces had ruled out any risk. It is unclear if this includes the plane from Madrid that had landed in Sofia.  Meanwhile, Czech police on Thursday said four planes headed to Prague received bomb threats and the authorities were preparing for their landing, adding they assessed the credibility of the threat s as low. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the threat , which is why all necessary security measures have been activated with minimal impact on passengers and airport operations," the police said on X.  "After landing, all aircraft will undergo pyrotechnic inspections."    CTK News agency later reported that no explosives were found in the four planes that landed in Prague, citing a police spokesperson.  Separately, t he Romanian intelligence agency said on Thursday that a bomb threat was made on a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest, adding the plane landed safely in the Romanian capital, Reuters reported.  Italy's ANSA news agency meanwhile reported on bomb alerts on two flights bound for Milan's Malpensa Airport, both of which have since landed safely.

A screengrab from a video shows a police officer and a sniffer dog inspecting a Ryanair airplane and its baggage, according to Guardia Civil, in Murcia, Spain, Nov 3, 2026. (Image: Reuters/Forta)

The string of incidents comes after about 10 European flights were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday , forcing the brief closure of a Warsaw airport and the scrambling of air force planes in Rome, according to authorities. No explosives were found in the earlier incidents, despite extensive searches on the ground after the planes all took off and landed safely in different European cities just several hours apart, AFP reported.  Irish budget carrier Ryanair appeared to be the worst hit, with four of its flights to different destinations being targeted. Two bomb warnings targeted planes heading to the Polish capital Warsaw, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and one from Heathrow operated by Polish airline LOT, Polish airport authorities said. This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of cheap, deniable disruption efforts. Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation, told Reuters the repeated threats could serve both to disrupt operations and to observe how airlines, airports and national authorities respond. "These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe," Almog said. "Different essential services are experiencing disruption that carries economic costs and can undermine public confidence."

Source: Agencies/lk/fs
